name: Karl Ziegler

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for meeting me, Karl. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions or political parties. What you say stays confidential. Could you describe a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I'm at a forty-person accounting firm in an old industrial town, and my clients are mostly manufacturers: metal fabricators, a brewery, a company that makes pumps. I do their year-end accounts and corporation tax, and I spend a lot of time on stock counts and machinery depreciation. Twice a year I'm on a factory floor in a hi-vis vest counting steel bar, which I actually enjoy.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What wears you out, and do you use any AI?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: Clients who change their stock figures three times in a week. I use the AI assistant the firm bought now and then, mostly to summarise long email chains, once the senior people said it was fine. In my spare time I'm treasurer of the local football club, so I do accounts for fun as well, which my girlfriend Anja finds hilarious.

S0.quote: The family that owns the pump maker has been with us thirty years, and the owner wants the same accountant at every March stock count, not a chatbot.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Mostly hype. I can believe that.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say the firm spent a lot of money on a fancy summary tool. At the football club I'd say good, the old ways still work. I might post a joke about it, but that's all.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I'd be relieved. My clients are family-owned manufacturers who like a face they know, and the firm is doing well. The family that owns the pump maker has been with us thirty years, and the owner wants the same accountant at every March stock count, not a chatbot.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep going exactly as I am and keep using the summary tool for long emails. Anja and I would keep saving five hundred a month for a house deposit. I'd aim to be manager within three years.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Comfortable. Like my plans still fit.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Anything weighing on you already?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: House prices, mostly. Anja's a nurse on shifts, and even with both our pay the deposit will take three more years. But my job feels safe.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you tell the partners the tool wasn't worth it?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: No, that's not my place. I'd just keep doing good work and let the numbers speak.

say: I'd joke that the firm paid for a **fancy summary tool**.
I'd tell the football club the **old ways** still work.
think: Long-standing **family manufacturers** want a familiar face, so I'd be relieved.
The firm is **doing well**, and my job feels secure.
do: Keep using the AI tool to **summarise emails**.
Save **£500 a month** with Anja towards a house deposit.
fieldNote: Karl's **secure** firm and loyal clients make this world easy for him.
His main pressure is **house prices**, not income.
Respects **hierarchy**: he wouldn't question the partners' purchase.

steps.text: Keep doing year-end accounts for the manufacturers
Save £500 a month with Anja for a house deposit
Work towards manager grade within three years

S1.quote: My dad lost his machinist job to a computer-controlled lathe, and I always thought sitting at a desk made me safe from that.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: That's more serious. Checking and planning is most of my week.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say the firm will adapt and good accountants will be fine. At the club I'd tell the lads it's like when the factories brought in machines, some jobs go, some come. I'd keep my head down online.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, I think the firm would hire fewer graduates and push more clients onto each of us. Corporation tax and depreciation schedules are exactly what a program does well. My dad lost his machinist job to a computer-controlled lathe, and I always thought sitting at a desk made me safe from that.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd take the firm's AI training once the senior people showed it works, and use the tools properly instead of now and then. I'd add another hundred a month to savings. And I'd make sure every client knows my name, so if the firm cut back, I'd be the one they'd ask for.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious, but not frozen.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said good accountants will be fine. Are you one of them?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'm average, honestly. Not bad, not the best. That's why I'd lean on the relationships.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What did your dad do after he lost that job?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: He went into maintenance at the same factory and fixed the lathe that replaced him. He always said learn the machine or it learns you.

say: I'd say the firm will **adapt** and good accountants will be fine.
I'd compare it to **factory machines**: some jobs go, some come.
think: The firm would hire **fewer graduates** and load more clients on each of us.
Desk work isn't **safe** after all, as my dad's lathe showed.
do: Join the firm's **AI training** once seniors prove it works.
Build **client relationships** so manufacturers ask for him by name.
fieldNote: His **father's story** frames everything: learn the machine or it learns you.
Admits he's **average**, so he bets on loyalty rather than skill.
Steady habit: adopts tools only after **seniors prove** them.

steps.text: Join the firm's AI training once seniors show it works
Add £100 a month to the house savings
Visit every manufacturing client in person this year

S2.quote: I'd rather be a twenty-seven-year-old apprentice with grease on my hands than an accountant waiting for a redundancy letter.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Two years? That changes everything.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say we need to look after our own people, our town and our families. I'd say the government should back apprenticeships, not just hand out cheques. At the club I'd try to keep the lads calm.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Truthfully, I'd expect the firm to cut most of us by 2029. The clients would love paying less, even the loyal ones. And thinking AI coming three years before the robots means the factory floor is safer than my desk for a while.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd pause the house deposit and keep it as cash, and cut the holiday and the car upgrade. I'd go straight to my dad's old factory and ask about a maintenance apprenticeship, even at a lower wage. Anja's nursing would carry us for a while.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Alarmed. My stomach drops just saying it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: An apprenticeship at twenty-seven, on lower pay. Could you really afford that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Only with Anja's wage and no house. I'd rather be a twenty-seven-year-old apprentice with grease on my hands than an accountant waiting for a redundancy letter.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell your father?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: That he was right. He'd probably be pleased in a strange way, and he'd teach me himself on Sundays.

say: I'd say we should **look after our own** people and town.
At the club I'd try to keep the **lads calm**.
think: The firm would **cut most of us** by 2029.
The **factory floor** is safer than my desk for about three years.
do: **Pause the deposit** and cut the holiday and car upgrade.
Ask for a **maintenance apprenticeship** at his dad's old factory.
Rely on **Anja's nursing** pay for a while.
fieldNote: Karl expects to **lose his job** and moves quickly toward hands-on work.
He uses the **robot gap** to justify an apprenticeship.
His **traditional views** shape what he asks for: apprenticeships over cheques.

steps.text: Pause the house purchase and keep the deposit as cash
Cancel the summer holiday and the car upgrade
Apply for a maintenance apprenticeship at his dad's old factory
Live on Anja's nursing wage during the apprenticeship

S3.quote: I'd rather own a small house before the storm than rent a nice flat through it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Five years. That's a bit more room.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say this is the time to plan, not to panic. At the club I'd organise a talk with someone from the local college about trades. I'd keep it practical.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I think I'd have about three good years at the firm, then it starts going. If I learn a hands-on skill now, I'd have until about 2034 when the robots come. That's a long enough runway to buy a house and get settled.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd buy the house in the next eighteen months while we both earn, something small near Anja's hospital. I'd start an evening course in industrial maintenance at the college in year two. And I'd keep using the AI tools at work, because it keeps me useful while I'm there.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Worried, but with a plan I believe in.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Isn't buying a house risky if your job ends by 2031?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A bit. But a small mortgage on a nurse's pay is manageable. I'd rather own a small house before the storm than rent a nice flat through it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who else at the firm would you warn?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The graduates. I'd tell them quietly to learn something with their hands as well, because they've got less experience to sell than me.

say: I'd say it's time to **plan, not panic**.
I'd organise a **trades talk** at the football club with the local college.
think: I'd have about **three good years** at the firm, then decline.
A **hands-on skill** gives me until about 2034.
do: Buy a **small house** near Anja's hospital within eighteen months.
Start an evening **industrial maintenance** course in year two.
Keep using **AI tools** at work while he's there.
feel: **Worried**, but holding a plan he **believes in**.
fieldNote: Five years lets Karl **buy a house** before switching careers.
He sizes the **mortgage** to his partner's nursing pay.
Thinks of **graduates** first when warning others.

steps.text: Buy a small house near Anja's hospital within eighteen months
Start an evening industrial maintenance course in year two
Keep using the firm's AI tools on client accounts

S4.quote: A job that's half spreadsheet and half factory floor buys me until the robots turn up, around 2039.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Ten years. Okay. That's a career's worth of planning.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say there's time, so get stuck in and prepare. At the club I'd say work hard and learn a skill. I wouldn't be calling for big government schemes.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I think I'd be fine for most of the decade. The owners of the family manufacturers I work with will want a person they trust for a long while. By the time AGI arrives, I'd want to be inside one of those firms, running the finance and the stores.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd buy the house in two years and become manager at the firm. Around 2030 I'd ask the pump maker, who's already hinted, about a finance and operations job. I'd learn the AI tools properly over the decade, once they're proven.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy, but I sleep fine.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said owners want a person. Won't AGI do the finance side by then?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Probably the numbers, yes. But the job I'd want is half on the factory floor, stores and stock and suppliers. A job that's half spreadsheet and half factory floor buys me until the robots turn up, around 2039.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would make you move sooner?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: If the firm stopped promoting people to manager. That would tell me they see no future for us.

say: I'd say there's **time**, so get stuck in and prepare.
I wouldn't call for **big government schemes**.
At the club I'd tell people to **learn a skill**.
think: I'd be **fine** for most of the decade.
By 2036 I'd want to be **inside a manufacturer**, running finance and stores.
do: Buy the **house** in two years and reach **manager** grade.
Ask the **pump maker** about a finance and operations job around 2030.
Learn AI tools **properly** once they're proven.
fieldNote: Karl expects his **income to hold** by moving into a client firm.
He picks a role **half hands-on** to use the robot gap.
Sets a **trigger**: the firm stopping manager promotions.

steps.text: Buy a house with Anja within two years
Get promoted to manager at the firm
Ask the pump maker about a finance and operations job
Learn the firm's AI tools properly once proven

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The two-year one. I'd be an apprentice at twenty-seven with no house and Anja carrying us. What would help is proper adult apprenticeships with a fair wage, paid by companies and government together, so people can learn a trade without losing everything.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Maybe about pride. My dad fixed the lathe that took his job, and I'd like to think I'd have the same pride if a machine took mine.

headlineQuote: My dad fixed the lathe that took his job, and I'd like to think I'd have the same pride if a machine took mine.
portrait: Karl is a **27-year-old accountant** serving family-owned manufacturers in an industrial town.
He lives with Anja, a **nurse**, and they're saving for a **house deposit**.
He uses AI **now and then**, once senior people say it's fine.
His dad's lost **machinist job** shapes his view: learn the machine or it learns you.
In every AGI picture he moves towards **hands-on work** or a factory-floor role.
biggestWorry: The **two-year** AGI picture, leaving him an apprentice with **no house**.
whatWouldHelp: **Adult apprenticeships** with a fair wage, paid by companies and government.
